Quantitative stability of optimal transport maps under variations of the target measure

Alex Delalande Address: Laboratoire de Mathématiques d’Orsay, Univ. Paris-Sud, CNRS, Université Paris-Saclay, 91405 Orsay, France and Inria Saclay, Ile-de-France and Quentin Mérigot Address: Laboratoire de Mathématiques d’Orsay, Univ. Paris-Sud, CNRS, Université Paris-Saclay, 91405 Orsay, France and Institut universitaire de France (IUF)
Abstract.

This work studies the quantitative stability of the quadratic optimal transport map between a fixed probability density ρ\rho and a probability measure μ\mu on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, which we denote TμT_{\mu}. Assuming that the source density ρ\rho is bounded from above and below on a compact convex set, we prove that the map μ↦Tμ\mu\mapsto T_{\mu} is bi-Hölder continuous on large families of probability measures, such as the set of probability measures whose moment of order p>dp>d is bounded by some constant. These stability estimates show that the linearized optimal transport metric W2,ρ​(μ,ν)=‖Tμ−Tν‖L2​(ρ,ℝd)\mathrm{W}_{2,\rho}(\mu,\nu)=\left\lVert T_{\mu}-T_{\nu}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{L}^{2}(\rho,\mathbb{R}^{d})} is bi-Hölder equivalent to the 22-Wasserstein distance on such sets, justifiying its use in applications.

1. Introduction

Let 𝒫2​(ℝd)\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) be the set of probability measures with finite second moment over ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} and ρ,μ∈𝒫2​(ℝd)\rho,\mu\in\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}). The optimal transport problem between ρ\rho and μ\mu with respect to the quadratic cost c⁡(x,y)=‖x−y‖2c(x,y)=\left\lVert x-y\right\rVert^{2} is the following minimization problem, where the minimum is taken over the set Π⁡(ρ,μ)\Pi(\rho,\mu) of transport plans between ρ\rho and μ\mu, that is the set of probability measures over ℝd×ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d} with marginals ρ\rho and μ\mu:

min⁡∫ℝd×ℝdγ∈Π⁡(ρ,μ)⁡‖x−y‖2​𝑑γ​(x,y).\displaystyle\min_{\gamma\in\Pi(\rho,\mu)}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}}\left\lVert x-y\right\rVert^{2}\mathrm{d}\gamma(x,y).

The square root of the value of this problem is called the 22-Wasserstein distance between ρ\rho and μ\mu and is denoted W2​(ρ,μ)\mathrm{W}_{2}(\rho,\mu). A theorem of Brenier [9] asserts that if ρ\rho is absolutely continuous with respect to the Lebesgue measure, the minimizer of the optimal transport problem is unique, and is induced by a map T=∇ϕT=\nabla\phi, where ϕ\phi is a convex function that verifies ∇ϕ#ρ=μ\nabla\phi_{\#}\rho=\mu. We recall that T#​ρT_{\#}\rho denotes the image measure of ρ\rho under the map TT. In our precise setting, where the density ρ\rho is bounded from above and below on a compact convex set, the potential ϕ\phi is uniquely defined in L2​(ρ)\mathrm{L}^{2}(\rho) up to an additional constant. Square-summability of ϕ\phi follows from the Poincaré-Wirtinger inequality on 𝒳\mathcal{X}.

Definition 1.1 (Potentials and maps).

We fix a probability measure ρ∈𝒫2​(ℝd)\rho\in\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}), which we assume to be absolutely continuous with respect to the Lebesgue measure and supported over a compact convex set 𝒳\mathcal{X}. We assume that the density of ρ\rho is bounded from above and below by positive constants on 𝒳\mathcal{X}. Given μ∈𝒫2​(ℝd),\mu\in\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}), we call

  • •

    Brenier map and denote TμT_{\mu} the (unique) optimal transport map between ρ\rho and μ\mu;

  • •

    Brenier potential the unique lower semi-continuous convex function ϕμ∈L2​(ρ)\phi_{\mu}\in\mathrm{L}^{2}(\rho) such that Tμ=∇ϕμT_{\mu}=\nabla\phi_{\mu} and which satisfies ∫𝒳ϕμ​𝑑ρ=0\int_{\mathcal{X}}\phi_{\mu}\mathrm{d}\rho=0;

  • •

    dual potential the convex conjugate of ϕμ\phi_{\mu}, denoted ψμ\psi_{\mu}:

    ∀y∈ℝd,ψμ​(y)=maxx∈𝒳⁡⟨x|y⟩−ϕμ​(x),\forall y\in\mathbb{R}^{d},\quad\psi_{\mu}(y)=\max_{x\in\mathcal{X}}\langle x|y\rangle-\phi_{\mu}(x),

    where the maximum is attained by lower semi-continuity of the convex function ϕμ\phi_{\mu} on the compact convex set 𝒳\mathcal{X}.

Since μ\mu is the image of ρ\rho under TμT_{\mu}, the mapping μ∈(𝒫2​(ℝd),W2)↦Tμ∈L2​(ρ,ℝd)\mu\in(\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}),\mathrm{W}_{2})\mapsto T_{\mu}\in\mathrm{L}^{2}(\rho,\mathbb{R}^{d}) is obviously injective. Using that (Tμ,Tν)#​ρ(T_{\mu},T_{\nu})_{\#}\rho is a coupling between μ\mu and ν\nu, one can actually prove that this mapping increases distances, namely

∀μ,ν∈𝒫2​(ℝd),W2​(μ,ν)≤‖Tμ−Tν‖L2​(ρ,ℝd).\forall\mu,\nu\in\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}),\quad\mathrm{W}_{2}(\mu,\nu)\leq\left\lVert T_{\mu}-T_{\nu}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{L}^{2}(\rho,\mathbb{R}^{d})}.

This mapping is also continuous: if a sequence of probability measures (μn)n(\mu_{n})_{n} converges to some μ\mu in (𝒫2​(ℝd),W2)(\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}),\mathrm{W}_{2}), then TμnT_{\mu_{n}} converges to TμT_{\mu} in L2​(ρ,ℝd)\mathrm{L}^{2}(\rho,\mathbb{R}^{d}). This continuity property is for instance implied by Corollary 5.23 in [37], together with the dominated convergence theorem. However, we note that the arguments used to prove this general continuity result are non-quantitative.

Linearized Optimal Transport

These two properties of the map μ↦Tμ\mu\mapsto T_{\mu} motivated its use to embed the metric space (𝒫2​(ℝd),W2)(\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}),\mathrm{W}_{2}) into the Hilbert space L2​(ρ,ℝd)\mathrm{L}^{2}(\rho,\mathbb{R}^{d}) [38].

This approach is often referred to as the Linearized Optimal Transport (LOT) framework and has shown great results in applications to image processing:

  • •

    [38, 23, 5, 11] used this idea to perform pattern recognition in images for various tasks, including discrimination of nuclear chromatin patterns in cancer cells, detection of differences in facial expressions, bird species, galaxy morphologies, sub-cellular protein distributions, detection and visualization of cell phenotype differences from microscopy images, or finally jets tagging of collider data in collider physics.

  • •

    [31] considered this framework for generative modelling of images, with experiments showcasing the generative modelling of digits and faces images, PET scans in the context of Alzheimer’s disease neuroimaging, or thyroid nuclei images.

  • •

    [22] followed this approach for improving the resolution of faces images.

At this stage, the good practical behavior of the linearized optimal transport framework is not justified from a mathematical viewpoint. A practical benefit of the embedding is to enable the use of the classical Hilbertian statistical toolbox on families of probability measures while keeping some features of the Wasserstein geometry. A particularly nice feature of the embedding μ↦Tμ\mu\mapsto T_{\mu} is that its image in L2​(ρ,ℝd)\mathrm{L}^{2}(\rho,\mathbb{R}^{d}) is convex, i.e. barycenters of optimal transport maps are optimal transport maps. Working with this embedding is equivalent to replacing the Wasserstein distance by the distance

W2,ρ​(μ,ν)=‖Tμ−Tν‖L2​(ρ,ℝd).\mathrm{W}_{2,\rho}(\mu,\nu)=\left\lVert T_{\mu}-T_{\nu}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{L}^{2}(\rho,\mathbb{R}^{d})}.

We note that the geodesic curves with respect to the distance W2,ρ\mathrm{W}_{2,\rho} are called the generalized geodesics in the book of Ambrosio, Gigli, Savaré [2]. The choice of the Brenier map between a reference measure ρ\rho and a measure μ\mu as an embedding of μ\mu may also be motivated by the Riemannian interpretation of the Wasserstein geometry [30, 2]. In this interpretation, the tangent space to 𝒫2​(ℝd)\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) at ρ\rho is included in L2​(ρ,ℝd)\mathrm{L}^{2}(\rho,\mathbb{R}^{d}). The Brenier map minus the identity, Tμ−idT_{\mu}-\mathrm{id}, can be regarded as the vector in the tangent space at ρ\rho which supports the Wasserstein geodesic from ρ\rho to μ\mu. In the Riemannian language again, the map μ↦Tμ−id\mu\mapsto T_{\mu}-\mathrm{id} would be called a logarithm, i.e. the inverse of the Riemannian exponential map: it sends a probability measure μ\mu in the (curved) manifold 𝒫2​(ℝd)\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) to a vector Tμ−idT_{\mu}-\mathrm{id} belonging to the linear space L2​(ρ,ℝd)\mathrm{L}^{2}(\rho,\mathbb{R}^{d}). This establishes a connection between the linearized optimal transport framework idea and similar strategies used to extend statistical inference notions such as principal component analysis to manifold-valued data, e.g. [17, 13].

It is quite natural to expect that the embedding μ↦Tμ\mu\mapsto T_{\mu} retains some of the geometry of the underlying space, or equivalently that the metric W2,ρ\mathrm{W}_{2,\rho} is comparable, in some coarse sense, to the Wasserstein distance. The main difficulty, which we study in this article, is to establish quantitative (e.g. Hölder) continuity properties for the mappings μ↦Tμ\mu\mapsto T_{\mu} and μ↦ϕμ\mu\mapsto\phi_{\mu}. We note that such stability estimates are also important in numerical analysis and in statistics, where a probability measure of interest μ∈𝒫2​(ℝd)\mu\in\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) is often approximated by a sequence of finitely supported measures (μn)n(\mu_{n})_{n}: convergence rates of quantities related to the sequence (Tμn)n(T_{\mu_{n}})_{n} toward a quantity related to TμT_{\mu} may then be directly deduced from quantitative stability estimates controlling ‖Tμn−Tμ‖L2​(ρ,ℝd)\left\lVert T_{\mu_{n}}-T_{\mu}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{L}^{2}(\rho,\mathbb{R}^{d})} with W2​(μn,μ)\mathrm{W}_{2}(\mu_{n},\mu).

Existing results

We focus here on the already known stability results on the mapping μ↦Tμ\mu\mapsto T_{\mu}, starting with negative results. We first note that explicit examples show that the mapping μ↦Tμ\mu\mapsto T_{\mu} is in general not better than 12\frac{1}{2}-Hölder, see §4 in [18] or Lemma 5.1 in [29]. A much stronger negative result comes from Andoni, Naor and Neiman [3, Theorem 7] showing that one cannot construct a bi-Hölder embedding of (𝒫2​(ℝd),W2),(\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}),\mathrm{W}_{2}), d≥3d\geq 3, into a Hilbert space:

Theorem (Andoni, Naor, Neiman).

(𝒫2​(ℝ3),W2)(\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{3}),\mathrm{W}_{2}) does not admit a uniform, coarse or quasisymmetric embedding into any Banach space of nontrivial type.

This theorem implies in particular that one cannot hope to prove that μ↦Tμ\mu\mapsto T_{\mu} is bi-Hölder on the whole set 𝒫2​(ℝd)\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) of probability measures with finite second moment.

Existing quantitative stability results can be summed up under the two following statements. A first result due to Ambrosio and reported in [18], shows a local 1/21/2-Hölder behaviour near probability densities μ\mu whose associated Brenier map TμT_{\mu} is Lipschitz continuous. We quote here a variant of this statement, from [29]:

Theorem (Ambrosio).

Let ρ\rho be a probability density over a compact set 𝒳\mathcal{X}. Let 𝒴⊂ℝd\mathcal{Y}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} be a compact set and μ,ν∈𝒫⁡(𝒴)\mu,\nu\in\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Y}). Assume that the Brenier map TμT_{\mu} from ρ\rho to μ\mu is LL-Lipschitz. Then,

‖Tμ−Tν‖L2​(ρ,ℝd)≤2​diam⁡(𝒳)​L​W1​(μ,ν)1/2.\|T_{\mu}-T_{\nu}\|_{\mathrm{L}^{2}(\rho,\mathbb{R}^{d})}\leq 2\sqrt{\diam(\mathcal{X})L}\mathrm{W}_{1}(\mu,\nu)^{1/2}.

Assuming Lipschitzness of the Brenier map is rather strong. First, it implies that the support of μ\mu is connected, so that the previous theorem cannot be applied when both μ\mu and ν\nu are finitely supported. In addition, to prove that TμT_{\mu} is Lipschitz one has to invoke the regularity theory for optimal transport maps, which requires very strong assumptions on μ\mu, in particular that its support spt⁡(μ)\spt(\mu) is convex. A more recent result, due to Berman [6], proves quantitative stability of the map μ↦Tμ\mu\mapsto T_{\mu} under milder assumptions on the target probability measures. Berman proves a stability result on the inverse transport maps when the target measure is bound to remain in a fixed compact set [6, Proposition 3.2]. This result implies quantitative stability of the Brenier maps; we refer to Corollary 2.4 in [29] for a precise statement.

Theorem (Berman).

Let ρ\rho be a probability density over a compact convex set 𝒳\mathcal{X}, bounded from above and below by positive constants. Let 𝒴\mathcal{Y} be a bounded connected open subset of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} with a Lipschitz boundary. Then there exists a constant CC depending only on ρ\rho, 𝒳\mathcal{X} and 𝒴\mathcal{Y} such that for any μ,ν∈𝒫⁡(𝒴)\mu,\nu\in\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Y}),

‖Tμ−Tν‖L2​(ρ,ℝd)≤C​W1​(μ,ν)12(d−1)​(d+2).\|T_{\mu}-T_{\nu}\|_{\mathrm{L}^{2}(\rho,\mathbb{R}^{d})}\leq C\mathrm{W}_{1}(\mu,\nu)^{\frac{1}{2^{(d-1)}(d+2)}}.

Unlike in Ambrosio’s theorem, the Hölder behavior given does not depend on the regularity of the transport map TμT_{\mu}. On the other hand, the Hölder exponent depends exponentially on the ambient dimension dd. As we will see below, this is not optimal.

Contributions

In this article, we prove quantitative stability results for quadratic optimal transport maps between a probability density ρ\rho and target measure μ\mu. We do not assume that μ\mu is compactly supported.

Introducing Mp​(μ)=∫ℝd‖x‖p​𝑑μ​(x)M_{p}(\mu)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\left\lVert x\right\rVert^{p}\mathrm{d}\mu(x) the pp-th moment of μ∈𝒫2​(ℝd)\mu\in\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}), we prove in particular the following theorem. We denote by Ca1,…,anC_{a_{1},\ldots,a_{n}} a non-negative constant which depends on a1,…,ana_{1},\ldots,a_{n}.

Theorem (Corollaries 3.4, 4.3 and 4.2).

Let 𝒳\mathcal{X} be a compact convex set and let ρ\rho be a probability density on 𝒳\mathcal{X}, bounded from above and below by positive constants. Let p>dp>d and p≥4p\geq 4. Assume that μ,ν∈𝒫2​(ℝd)\mu,\nu\in\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) have bounded pp-th moment, i.e. max⁡(Mp​(μ),Mp​(ν))≤Mp<+∞\max(M_{p}(\mu),M_{p}(\nu))\leq M_{p}<+\infty. Then

‖Tμ−Tν‖L2​(ρ,ℝd)≤Cd,p,𝒳,ρ,Mp​W1​(μ,ν)p6​p+16​d,\left\lVert T_{\mu}-T_{\nu}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{L}^{2}(\rho,\mathbb{R}^{d})}\leq C_{d,p,\mathcal{X},\rho,M_{p}}\mathrm{W}_{1}(\mu,\nu)^{\frac{p}{6p+16d}},
‖ϕμ−ϕν‖L2​(ρ)≤Cd,p,𝒳,ρ,Mp​W1​(μ,ν)1/2.\left\lVert\phi_{\mu}-\phi_{\nu}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{L}^{2}(\rho)}\leq C_{d,p,\mathcal{X},\rho,M_{p}}\mathrm{W}_{1}(\mu,\nu)^{1/2}.

If μ,ν\mu,\nu are supported on a compact set 𝒴\mathcal{Y}, we have an improved Hölder exponent for the Brenier map:

‖Tμ−Tν‖L2​(ρ,ℝd)≤Cd,𝒳,𝒴,ρ​W1​(μ,ν)16.\left\lVert T_{\mu}-T_{\nu}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{L}^{2}(\rho,\mathbb{R}^{d})}\leq C_{d,\mathcal{X},\mathcal{Y},\rho}\mathrm{W}_{1}(\mu,\nu)^{\frac{1}{6}}.
Remark 1.1 (Comparison between W1\mathrm{W}_{1} and W2\mathrm{W}_{2}).

We note that since W1≤W2\mathrm{W}_{1}\leq\mathrm{W}_{2}, the estimates in all the previous theorems indeed imply a bi-Hölder behaviour of the map μ↦Tμ\mu\mapsto T_{\mu} on subsets of 𝒫2​(ℝd)\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) with respect to both Wasserstein distances W1\mathrm{W}_{1} and W2\mathrm{W}_{2}.

Remark 1.2 (Constants).

The constants appearing in the above theorem may all be tracked down and all feature the product of three terms that depend respectively on the dimension dd, the diameter and perimeter of 𝒳\mathcal{X}, and the bounds mρ,Mρ>0m_{\rho},M_{\rho}>0 on ρ\rho that are such that mρ≤ρ≤Mρm_{\rho}\leq\rho\leq M_{\rho} on 𝒳\mathcal{X}. If μ,ν\mu,\nu are supported on a compact set 𝒴\mathcal{Y}, the constants also feature a factor that only depends on the smallest positive real R𝒴R_{\mathcal{Y}} such that 𝒴⊂B⁡(0,R𝒴)\mathcal{Y}\subset B(0,R_{\mathcal{Y}}). For instance in such compact setting, the constant controlling the L2​(ρ)\mathrm{L}^{2}(\rho) distance between ϕμ\phi_{\mu} and ϕν\phi_{\nu} reads:

Cd,p,𝒳,ρ,Mp=Cd,p,𝒳,ρ,𝒴=e⁡(d+1)​2d​Mρ2mρ2​diam⁡(𝒳)2​R𝒴.C_{d,p,\mathcal{X},\rho,M_{p}}=C_{d,p,\mathcal{X},\rho,\mathcal{Y}}=e(d+1)2^{d}\frac{M_{\rho}^{2}}{m_{\rho}^{2}}\diam(\mathcal{X})^{2}R_{\mathcal{Y}}.

In the non-compact setting, a factor involving MpM_{p} appears, as well as a factor involving the Poincaré constant of order pp of 𝒳\mathcal{X} and the pp-th power of the ratio R𝒳r𝒳\frac{R_{\mathcal{X}}}{r_{\mathcal{X}}}, where r𝒳,R𝒳>0r_{\mathcal{X}},R_{\mathcal{X}}>0 are the largest and smallest reals such that B⁡(0,r𝒳)⊂𝒳⊂B⁡(0,R𝒳)B(0,r_{\mathcal{X}})\subset\mathcal{X}\subset B(0,R_{\mathcal{X}}) (assuming without any loss of generality 𝒳\mathcal{X} contains the origin).

A large class of probability measures verifies the moment assumption, such as sub-Gaussian or sub-exponential measures (see Remark 3.1). A preliminary version of this theorem was announced in [29], with a different proof strategy, relying on the study of the case where both μ,ν\mu,\nu are supported on the same finite set. The proof in [29] led to a worse Hölder exponent in the compact case, and couldn’t deal with non-compactly supported measures. We do not know whether the Hölder exponents in this theorem are optimal.

To prove these stability estimates, we use the fact that the dual potentials solve a convex minimization problem involving the functional 𝒦⁡(ψ)=∫ψ∗​𝑑ρ\mathcal{K}(\psi)=\int\psi^{*}\mathrm{d}\rho, which we call Kantorovich’s functional. We first prove in (§2) a strong convexity estimate for Kantorovich’s functional, relying in particular on the Brascamp-Lieb inequality, and which holds under the assumption that the Brenier potentials are bounded. This strong convexity estimate is then translated into a stability estimate concerning the dual and Brenier potentials (§3). The stability of Brenier maps is then obtained (§4), relying in particular on a Gagliardo-Nirenberg type inequality for the difference of convex functions (§5), which might be of independent interest.

2. Strong convexity of Kantorovich’s functional

Let 𝒳\mathcal{X} be a compact convex subset of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, and let ρ\rho be a probability density on 𝒳\mathcal{X}. Given any measure μ∈𝒫2​(ℝd)\mu\in\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}), we consider the problem of finding the coupling γ∈Π⁡(ρ,μ)\gamma\in\Pi(\rho,\mu) which maximizes the correlation ∫⟨x|y⟩​𝑑γ​(x,y)\int\langle x|y\rangle\mathrm{d}\gamma(x,y). This problem is equivalent to the standard quadratic optimal transport problem and in this setting Kantorovich duality reads

max⁡∫γ∈Π⁡(ρ,μ)⁡⟨x|y⟩​𝑑γ​(x,y)=minψ∈𝒞0​(ℝd)⁡𝒦⁡(ψ)+∫ℝdψ​𝑑μ,\max_{\gamma\in\Pi(\rho,\mu)}\int\langle x|y\rangle\mathrm{d}\gamma(x,y)=\min_{\psi\in\mathcal{C}^{0}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}\mathcal{K}(\psi)+\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\psi\mathrm{d}\mu,

where the functional 𝒦\mathcal{K}, which we will call Kantorovich’s functional, is defined by

𝒦⁡(ψ):=∫𝒳ψ∗​𝑑ρ.\displaystyle\mathcal{K}(\psi):=\int_{\mathcal{X}}\psi^{*}\mathrm{d}\rho.

This dual formulation of the maximal correlation problem can for instance be found as Particular Case 5.16 in [37]. Kantorovichs’ functional is convex because for any x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, the map ψ↦ψ∗​(x)\psi\mapsto\psi^{*}(x) is convex in ψ\psi. Moreover, formal computations, which are justified in Proposition 2.2, show that

∇𝒦​(ψ)=−(∇ψ∗)#​ρ.\nabla\mathcal{K}(\psi)=-(\nabla\psi^{*})_{\#}\rho.

In particular, with ϕμ\phi_{\mu} the Brenier potential associated to the optimal transport problem between ρ\rho and μ\mu and ψμ=ϕμ∗\psi_{\mu}=\phi_{\mu}^{*} its convex conjugate, this gives the relation ψμ=(∇𝒦)−1​(−μ)\psi_{\mu}=(\nabla\mathcal{K})^{-1}(-\mu). Since 𝒦\mathcal{K} is convex, its gradient must be monotone, thus implying that for all probability measures μ0,μ1∈𝒫2​(ℝd)\mu^{0},\mu^{1}\in\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}),

⟨ψμ1−ψμ0|∇𝒦​(ψμ1)−∇𝒦​(ψμ0)⟩=⟨ψμ1−ψμ0|μ0−μ1⟩≥0.\langle\psi_{\mu^{1}}-\psi_{\mu^{0}}|\nabla\mathcal{K}(\psi_{\mu^{1}})-\nabla\mathcal{K}(\psi_{\mu^{0}})\rangle=\langle\psi_{\mu^{1}}-\psi_{\mu^{0}}|\mu^{0}-\mu^{1}\rangle\geq 0.

Our aim in this section is to prove Theorem 2.1, establishing strong convexity estimates for Kantorovich’s functional 𝒦\mathcal{K}, which we will later be able to translate into stability estimates for μ↦ψμ=(∇𝒦)−1​(−μ).\mu\mapsto\psi_{\mu}=(\nabla\mathcal{K})^{-1}(-\mu).

Theorem 2.1 (Strong convexity).

Let μ0,μ1∈𝒫2​(ℝd)\mu^{0},\mu^{1}\in\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) and let ρ\rho be a probability density over a compact convex set 𝒳\mathcal{X}, satisfying 0<mρ≤ρ≤Mρ0<m_{\rho}\leq\rho\leq M_{\rho}. For k∈{0,1}k\in\{0,1\}, denote ϕk=ϕμk\phi^{k}=\phi_{\mu^{k}} the Brenier potential between ρ\rho and μk\mu^{k} (see Definition 1.1). Assume that

(1) ∀k∈{0,1},−∞<mϕ≤min𝒳⁡ϕk≤max𝒳⁡ϕk≤Mϕ<+∞.\forall k\in\{0,1\},\quad-\infty<m_{\phi}\leq\min_{\mathcal{X}}\phi^{k}\leq\max_{\mathcal{X}}\phi^{k}\leq M_{\phi}<+\infty.

Then the convex conjugates ψ0\psi^{0} and ψ1\psi^{1} of ϕ0\phi^{0} and ϕ1\phi^{1} verify:

(2) Var12​(μ0+μ1)⁡(ψ1−ψ0)≤Cd​Mρ2mρ2​(Mϕ−mϕ)​⟨ψ0−ψ1|μ1−μ0⟩,\Var_{\frac{1}{2}(\mu^{0}+\mu^{1})}(\psi^{1}-\psi^{0})\leq C_{d}\frac{M_{\rho}^{2}}{m_{\rho}^{2}}(M_{\phi}-m_{\phi})\langle\psi^{0}-\psi^{1}|\mu^{1}-\mu^{0}\rangle,

where Cd=e⁡(d+1)​2d−1C_{d}=e(d+1)2^{d-1}.

Remark 2.1 (Variance).

The left-hand side of (2) involves the variance of ψ1−ψ0\psi^{1}-\psi^{0} instead of a squared L2\mathrm{L}^{2} norm. This is to be expected, because of the invariance of the Kantorovich’s functional under addition of a constant. The choice of μ0+μ1\mu_{0}+\mu_{1} as the reference measure for the variance term in inequality (2) may seem unnatural, but we note that there is no natural reference measure on the target. The choice of 12​(μ0+μ1)\frac{1}{2}(\mu^{0}+\mu^{1}) as the reference measures proves relevant for establishing the stability of Brenier potentials in the next section. Proposition 3.1 especially asserts that Var12​(μ0+μ1)⁡(ψ1−ψ0)≥12​Varρ⁡(ϕ1−ϕ0)\Var_{\frac{1}{2}(\mu^{0}+\mu^{1})}(\psi^{1}-\psi^{0})\geq\frac{1}{2}\Var_{\rho}(\phi^{1}-\phi^{0}). We also note that, as detailed in the proof of Theorem 2.1, the left-hand side of the inequality could actually be replaced by the quantity

Cd​Mρmρ​∫01Varμt⁡(ψ1−ψ0)​𝑑t,C_{d}\frac{M_{\rho}}{m_{\rho}}\int_{0}^{1}\Var_{\mu^{t}}(\psi^{1}-\psi^{0})\mathrm{d}t,

where for t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1], μt=∇((1−t)ψ0+tψ1)#∗ρ\mu^{t}=\nabla((1-t)\psi^{0}+t\psi^{1})^{*}_{\#}\rho interpolates between μ0\mu^{0} and μ1\mu^{1}. This inequality is tighter, but the interpolation t↦μtt\mapsto\mu_{t} has no simple interpretation and is quite difficult to manipulate. In particular, this curve is not a generalized geodesic in the sense of Ambrosio, Gigli, Savaré [2].

Remark 2.2 (Optimality of exponents).

Estimate (2) is optimal in term of exponent of Var12​(μ0+μ1)⁡(ψ1−ψ0)\Var_{\frac{1}{2}(\mu^{0}+\mu^{1})}(\psi^{1}-\psi^{0}). Indeed in dimension d=1d=1, for ε≥0\varepsilon\geq 0, denote με\mu_{\varepsilon} the uniform probability measure on the segment [ε,1+ε][\varepsilon,1+\varepsilon]. Then for ρ=μ0\rho=\mu_{0}, one can show that for ε≤1\varepsilon\leq 1, both Var12​(μ0+με)⁡(ψε−ψ0)\Var_{\frac{1}{2}(\mu^{0}+\mu^{\varepsilon})}(\psi^{\varepsilon}-\psi^{0}) and ⟨ψ0−ψε|με−μ0⟩\langle\psi^{0}-\psi^{\varepsilon}|\mu^{\varepsilon}-\mu^{0}\rangle are of the order of ε2\varepsilon^{2}.

The strong convexity estimate of Theorem 2.1 may find applications beyond the stability of optimal transport maps. In particular, the authors noticed in a subsequent work [12] that this estimate can be used to derive non-trivial quantitative stability bounds for Wasserstein barycenters (defined in [1]) under mild regularity assumptions on the marginal measures.

We also note that a strong convexity estimate similar to (2) was derived in [16] for entropy-regularized optimal transport, using a proof similar in spirit to the proof of Theorem 2.1 to be presented below.

The strong convexity estimate (2) is derived from a local estimate, a Poincaré-Wirtinger inequality for the second derivative of 𝒦\mathcal{K}, which is in turn a consequence of the Brascamp-Lieb inequality (5). To make the connection with the Brascamp-Lieb inequality clearer, we first compute the first and second order derivatives of 𝒦\mathcal{K} along the path ((1−t)​ψ0+t​ψ1)t∈[0,1]((1-t)\psi^{0}+t\psi^{1})_{t\in[0,1]}, under regularity and strong convexity hypotheses. These hypothesis are relaxed in the proof of Theorem 2.1.

Proposition 2.2.

Let ϕ0,ϕ1∈𝒞2​(ℝd)\phi^{0},\phi^{1}\in\mathcal{C}^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) be strongly convex functions. Define ψ0=(ϕ0)∗\psi^{0}=(\phi^{0})^{*}, ψ1=(ϕ1)∗\psi^{1}=(\phi^{1})^{*} and v=ψ1−ψ0v=\psi^{1}-\psi^{0}. Then, ϕt\phi^{t} is a strongly convex function, belongs to 𝒞2​(ℝd)\mathcal{C}^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}), and

(3) dd​t​𝒦​(ψt)\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\mathcal{K}(\psi^{t}) =−∫𝒳v(∇ϕt(x))dρ(x),\displaystyle=-\int_{\mathcal{X}}v(\nabla\phi^{t}(x))\mathrm{d}\rho(x),

We then find a positive lower-bound on the second order derivative expressed in equation (4) using the Brascamp-Lieb inequality [8]. We cite here a version of this inequality that is adapted to our context, i.e. that concerns log-concave probability measures supported on the compact and convex set 𝒳\mathcal{X}. This statement is a special case of Corollary 1.3 of [24], where 𝒳\mathcal{X} is a convex subset of a Riemannian manifold. We also refer to Section 3.1.1 of [21].

To deduce the general case of Theorem 2.1, we need to approximate the convex potentials ϕ0,ϕ1\phi^{0},\phi^{1} on 𝒳\mathcal{X} with strongly convex potentials ϕn0,ϕn1\phi^{0}_{n},\phi^{1}_{n} that belong to 𝒞2​(𝒳)\mathcal{C}^{2}(\mathcal{X}) and that are such that their gradients ∇ϕn0,∇ϕn1\nabla\phi^{0}_{n},\nabla\phi^{1}_{n} induce diffeomorphisms between 𝒳\mathcal{X} and a closed ball 𝒴n\mathcal{Y}_{n}. A regularization that uses a (standard) convolution does not seem directly feasible. Indeed, ϕk\phi^{k} is defined on 𝒳\mathcal{X} only, and its gradient explodes on the boundary of 𝒳\mathcal{X} when μk\mu^{k} has non-compact support, so that any convex extension of ϕk\phi^{k} to ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} has to take value +∞+\infty.

Our strategy is as follows. First, we resort to Moreau-Yosida’s regularization to approximate the functions ϕ0,ϕ1\phi^{0},\phi^{1} by regular convex functions defined on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. Then, we regularize the target probability measures associated to the approximated potentials and resort to Caffarelli’s regularity theory to guarantee smoothness and strong convexity. Caffarelli’s regularity theory results require smoothness assumptions on the source probability measure and strong convexity and smoothness assumption on the domain. We make these assumptions in the next proposition, but we will later show that these can be relaxed to get the general case of Theorem 2.1.

Proposition 2.5.

Let μ0,μ1∈𝒫2​(ℝd)\mu^{0},\mu^{1}\in\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}). Let 𝒳\mathcal{X} be a compact, smooth and strongly convex set, let ρ\rho be a smooth probability density on 𝒳\mathcal{X} and assume that ρ\rho is bounded away from zero and infinity on this set. Denote ϕk\phi^{k} the Brenier potentials for the quadratic optimal transport from ρ\rho to μk\mu^{k}, ψk=(ϕk)∗\psi^{k}=(\phi^{k})^{*}, and assume that there exists mϕ,Mϕ∈ℝm_{\phi},M_{\phi}\in\mathbb{R} such for k∈{0,1}k\in\{0,1\} and any x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X},

mϕ≤ϕk​(x)≤Mϕ.m_{\phi}\leq\phi^{k}(x)\leq M_{\phi}.

Then there exists sequences of strongly convex functions (ϕn0)n∈ℕ,(ϕn1)n∈ℕ(\phi^{0}_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}},(\phi^{1}_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}} in 𝒞2​(ℝd)\mathcal{C}^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) such that if one introduces μkn=∇ϕkn​#ρ\mu^{k}_{n}=\nabla\phi^{k}_{n\#}\rho and ψnk=(ϕnk)∗\psi^{k}_{n}=(\phi^{k}_{n})^{*}, then:

  1. (i)

    limn→+∞⟨ψn0−ψn1|μn1−μn0⟩=⟨ψ0−ψ1|μ1−μ0⟩\lim_{n\to+\infty}\langle\psi^{0}_{n}-\psi^{1}_{n}|\mu^{1}_{n}-\mu^{0}_{n}\rangle=\langle\psi^{0}-\psi^{1}|\mu^{1}-\mu^{0}\rangle,

  2. (ii)

    limn→+∞Var12​(μn0+μn1)⁡(ψn1−ψn0)=Var12​(μ0+μ1)⁡(ψ1−ψ0)\lim_{n\to+\infty}\Var_{\frac{1}{2}(\mu^{0}_{n}+\mu^{1}_{n})}(\psi^{1}_{n}-\psi^{0}_{n})=\Var_{\frac{1}{2}(\mu^{0}+\mu^{1})}(\psi^{1}-\psi^{0}),

  3. (iii)

    let mϕn=min𝒳⁡mink​ϕnk{m_{\phi}}_{n}=\min_{\mathcal{X}}\min_{k}\phi^{k}_{n}, and Mϕn=max𝒳⁡maxk​ϕnk{M_{\phi}}_{n}=\max_{\mathcal{X}}\max_{k}\phi^{k}_{n}. Then,

    mϕ≤lim infn→+∞mϕn≤lim supn→+∞Mϕn≤Mϕm_{\phi}\leq\liminf_{n\to+\infty}{m_{\phi}}_{n}\leq\limsup_{n\to+\infty}{M_{\phi}}_{n}\leq M_{\phi}
  4. (iv)

    there exists a closed ball 𝒴n\mathcal{Y}_{n} such that for k∈{0,1}k\in\{0,1\}, ∇ϕnk\nabla\phi^{k}_{n} is a diffeomorphism between 𝒳\mathcal{X} and 𝒴n\mathcal{Y}_{n}.

Before proving this proposition, we recall some facts regarding Moreau-Yosida’s regularization of convex functions. Quoting Section 3.4 of [4], the Moreau-Yosida regularization of parameter λ>0\lambda>0 of a closed and proper convex function f:ℝd→ℝ∪{+∞}f:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\} is defined for all x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d} by infimum convolution of the function ff with 12​λ​‖⋅‖2\frac{1}{2\lambda}\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert^{2}:

fλ​(x)\displaystyle f_{\lambda}(x) =minu∈ℝd⁡f⁡(u)+12​λ​‖u−x‖2.\displaystyle=\min_{u\in\mathbb{R}^{d}}f(u)+\frac{1}{2\lambda}\left\lVert u-x\right\rVert^{2}.

The next lemma gathers a few properties of the Moreau-Yosida regularisation.

Lemma 2.6.

Let f:ℝd→ℝ∪{+∞}f:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\} be a closed and proper convex function and let λ>0\lambda>0. Then,

  1. (i)

    fλ=(f∗+λ2​‖⋅‖2)∗f_{\lambda}=(f^{*}+\frac{\lambda}{2}\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert^{2})^{*},

  2. (ii)

    for all x∈ℝd,x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, limλ→0fλ​(x)=f⁡(x),\lim_{\lambda\to 0}f_{\lambda}(x)=f(x),

  3. (iii)

    fλ∈𝒞1,1​(ℝd)f_{\lambda}\in\mathcal{C}^{1,1}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) and more precisely, ∇fλ\nabla f_{\lambda} is 1λ\frac{1}{\lambda}-Lipschitz,

  4. (iv)

    if ff is differentiable at x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, then limλ→0∇fλ​(x)=∇f​(x),\lim_{\lambda\to 0}\nabla f_{\lambda}(x)=\nabla f(x),

  5. (v)

    if ff is differentiable at x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, then ‖∇fλ​(x)‖≤‖∇f​(x)‖\left\lVert\nabla f_{\lambda}(x)\right\rVert\leq\left\lVert\nabla f(x)\right\rVert.

Proof.

Point (i) is found in Proposition 3.3 of [4], points (ii) and (iii) are found in Theorem 3.24 of [4] and (iv) and (v) can be found in Proposition 2.6 of [10]. ∎

Proposition 2.7.

In addition to the assumptions of Theorem 2.1, assume that 𝒳\mathcal{X} is a smooth and strongly convex set and that the density ρ\rho is smooth. Then, (2) holds.

Proof.

Let ϕn0,ϕn1\phi^{0}_{n},\phi^{1}_{n} be the sequence of 𝒞2\mathcal{C}^{2} and strongly convex potentials constructed by Proposition 2.5, converging respectively to ϕ0\phi^{0} and ϕ1\phi^{1}, and such that ∇ϕn0,∇ϕn1\nabla\phi^{0}_{n},\nabla\phi^{1}_{n} are diffeomorphisms from 𝒳\mathcal{X} to a ball 𝒴n\mathcal{Y}_{n}. By Proposition 2.4, (2) holds for ϕn0,ϕn1\phi^{0}_{n},\phi^{1}_{n}:

Varμn0+μn1⁡(ψn1−ψn0)≤Cd​Mρ2mρ2​(Mϕn−mϕn)​⟨ψn0−ψn1|μn1−μn0⟩.\Var_{\mu^{0}_{n}+\mu^{1}_{n}}(\psi^{1}_{n}-\psi^{0}_{n})\leq C_{d}\frac{M_{\rho}^{2}}{m_{\rho}^{2}}({M_{\phi}}_{n}-{m_{\phi}}_{n})\langle\psi^{0}_{n}-\psi^{1}_{n}|\mu^{1}_{n}-\mu^{0}_{n}\rangle.

By the claims (i)-(iv) in Proposition 2.5, all the terms in this inequality converge as n→+∞n\to+\infty and establish (2) in the limit. ∎

Let KK be a smooth, non-negative and compactly supported function, Kn​(x)=nd​K​(n​x)K_{n}(x)=n^{d}K(nx) and define

ρn=1Zn​(ρ∗Kn)|𝒳n,mρn=mρZn,Mρn=MρZn,\rho_{n}=\frac{1}{Z_{n}}\left.(\rho*K_{n})\right|_{\mathcal{X}_{n}},{m_{\rho}}_{n}=\frac{m_{\rho}}{Z_{n}},{M_{\rho}}_{n}=\frac{M_{\rho}}{Z_{n}},

where ZnZ_{n} is a constant ensuring that ρn\rho_{n} belongs to 𝒫⁡(𝒳n)\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{X}_{n}). We define μkn=∇ϕk#ρn\mu^{k}_{n}=\nabla\phi^{k}_{\#}\rho_{n}. Applying Proposition 2.7 to (𝒳n,ρn)(\mathcal{X}_{n},\rho_{n}) and (ϕ0,ϕ1)(\phi^{0},\phi^{1}), we have:

(14) Varμn0+μn1⁡(ψ1−ψ0)≤Cd​Mρn2mρn2​(Mϕ−mϕ)​⟨ψ0−ψ1|μn1−μn0⟩.\Var_{\mu^{0}_{n}+\mu^{1}_{n}}(\psi^{1}-\psi^{0})\leq C_{d}\frac{{M_{\rho}}_{n}^{2}}{{m_{\rho}}_{n}^{2}}(M_{\phi}-m_{\phi})\langle\psi^{0}-\psi^{1}|\mu^{1}_{n}-\mu^{0}_{n}\rangle.

By construction, limn→+∞Zn=1\lim_{n\to+\infty}Z_{n}=1 and ρn\rho_{n} converges to ρ\rho in L1​(𝒳)\mathrm{L}^{1}(\mathcal{X}). Thus up to subsequences, ρn\rho_{n} converges pointwise almost everywhere to ρ\rho. Setting f=ψ0−ψ1f=\psi^{0}-\psi^{1}, we have

⟨ψ0−ψ1​|μn0⟩=∫𝒳f⁡(∇ϕ0)​ρn​(x)​𝑑x→n→+∞∫𝒳f⁡(∇ϕ0)​ρ​(x)​𝑑x=⟨ψ0−ψ1|​μ0⟩.\langle\psi^{0}-\psi^{1}|\mu^{0}_{n}\rangle=\int_{\mathcal{X}}f(\nabla\phi^{0})\rho_{n}(x)\mathrm{d}x\xrightarrow{n\to+\infty}\int_{\mathcal{X}}f(\nabla\phi^{0})\rho(x)\mathrm{d}x=\langle\psi^{0}-\psi^{1}|\mu^{0}\rangle.

The limit in the above equation is proven as in Proposition 2.5, using that ff is Lipschitz, that M2​(μ0)<+∞M_{2}(\mu_{0})<+\infty and applying the dominated convergence theorem. All the terms can be dealt with in a similar manner. Taking the limit n→+∞n\to+\infty in (14) gives the desired (2). ∎

3. Stability of potentials

A direct consequence of the strong convexity estimate of Theorem 2.1 is a quantitative stability result on the dual potential ψμ\psi_{\mu} with respect to the target measure μ\mu. This estimate on dual potentials is readily transferred to the Brenier (primal) potentials thanks to the next proposition. We refer to Definition 1.1 for a definition of the potentials.

Proposition 3.1.

Let ρ\rho be a probability density over a compact convex set 𝒳\mathcal{X}, and let ϕ0,ϕ1\phi^{0},\phi^{1} be convex functions on 𝒳\mathcal{X}. Denote ψk\psi^{k} the convex conjugate of ϕk\phi^{k} and μk\mu^{k} the image of ρ\rho under ∇ϕk\nabla\phi^{k}. Then for any p>0p>0,

‖ϕ1−ϕ0‖Lp​(ρ)≤‖ψ1−ψ0‖Lp​(μ0+μ1).\left\lVert\phi^{1}-\phi^{0}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{L}^{p}(\rho)}\leq\left\lVert\psi^{1}-\psi^{0}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{L}^{p}(\mu^{0}+\mu^{1})}.

In particular,

12​Varρ⁡(ϕ1−ϕ0)≤Var12​(μ0+μ1)⁡(ψ1−ψ0).\frac{1}{2}\Var_{\rho}(\phi^{1}-\phi^{0})\leq\Var_{\frac{1}{2}(\mu^{0}+\mu^{1})}(\psi^{1}-\psi^{0}).

Before proving this proposition, let us mention some consequences. The stability estimates resulting from Theorem 2.1 and this proposition are expressed in Corollary 3.2 in terms of variance for the potentials and 11-Wasserstein distance for the target measures. Assuming that one of the target measures is absolutely continuous with respect to the other, these estimates can also be expressed in term of χ2\chi^{2} or Kagan’s divergence of the target measures. The χ2\chi^{2} divergence reduces to the χ2\chi^{2} test-statistic used for goodness of fit testing when the compared measures are finitely and commonly supported and one of them is observed empirically. Note that such divergence can be interpreted as the square of a divergence, noting for instance that the total variation distance is only 12\frac{1}{2}-Hölder stable with respect to it [32].

Corollary 3.2 (Stability of potentials).

Let ρ\rho be a probability density over a compact convex set 𝒳\mathcal{X}, satisfying 0<mρ≤ρ≤Mρ0<m_{\rho}\leq\rho\leq M_{\rho} and let μ0,μ1∈𝒫2​(ℝd)\mu^{0},\mu^{1}\in\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}). For k∈{0,1}k\in\{0,1\}, denote ϕk=ϕμk\phi^{k}=\phi_{\mu^{k}} the Brenier potential between ρ\rho and μk\mu^{k}. Assume that ϕ0,ϕ1\phi^{0},\phi^{1} satisfy (1) and denote ψ0\psi^{0} and ψ1\psi^{1} the convex conjugates of ϕ0\phi^{0} and ϕ1\phi^{1}. Then,

Varρ⁡(ϕ1−ϕ0)≤2​Var12​(μ0+μ1)⁡(ψ1−ψ0)≤Cd,ρ​diam⁡(𝒳)​(Mϕ−mϕ)​W1​(μ0,μ1)\Var_{\rho}(\phi^{1}-\phi^{0})\leq 2\Var_{\frac{1}{2}(\mu^{0}+\mu^{1})}(\psi^{1}-\psi^{0})\leq C_{d,\rho}\diam(\mathcal{X})(M_{\phi}-m_{\phi})\mathrm{W}_{1}(\mu^{0},\mu^{1})

with Cd,ρ=e⁡(d+1)​2d​Mρ2mρ2C_{d,\rho}=e(d+1)2^{d}\frac{M_{\rho}^{2}}{m_{\rho}^{2}}. Assuming additionally that μ1\mu^{1} is absolutely continuous w.r.t. μ0\mu^{0}, then

Varρ⁡(ϕ1−ϕ0)≤2​Var12​(μ0+μ1)⁡(ψ1−ψ0)≤Cd,ρ2​(Mϕ−mϕ)2​Dχ2​(μ1|μ0)\Var_{\rho}(\phi^{1}-\phi^{0})\leq 2\Var_{\frac{1}{2}(\mu^{0}+\mu^{1})}(\psi^{1}-\psi^{0})\leq C_{d,\rho}^{2}(M_{\phi}-m_{\phi})^{2}D_{\chi^{2}}(\mu^{1}|\mu^{0})

where Dχ2​(μ1|μ0)D_{\chi^{2}}(\mu^{1}|\mu^{0}) stands for the χ2\chi^{2} or Kagan’s divergence from μ1\mu^{1} to μ0\mu^{0}.

Proof.

Proposition 3.1 combined with Theorem 2.1 give the inequalities

Varρ⁡(ϕ1−ϕ0)\displaystyle\Var_{\rho}(\phi^{1}-\phi^{0}) ≤2​Var12​(μ0+μ1)⁡(ψ1−ψ0)\displaystyle\leq 2\Var_{\frac{1}{2}(\mu^{0}+\mu^{1})}(\psi^{1}-\psi^{0})
≤Cd,ρ​(Mϕ−mϕ)​⟨ψ0−ψ1|μ1−μ0⟩.\displaystyle\leq C_{d,\rho}(M_{\phi}-m_{\phi})\langle\psi^{0}-\psi^{1}|\mu^{1}-\mu^{0}\rangle.

The first estimate follows from Kantorovich-Rubinstein duality result: for any x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and k∈{0,1}k\in\{0,1\}, for any gk∈∂ψk​(x)g^{k}\in\partial\psi^{k}(x), one has gk∈𝒳g^{k}\in\mathcal{X} so that ψ1−ψ0\psi^{1}-\psi^{0} is diam⁡(𝒳)\diam(\mathcal{X})-Lipschitz continuous. Kantorovich-Rubinstein duality formula then ensures

⟨ψ0−ψ1|μ1−μ0⟩≤diam⁡(𝒳)​W1​(μ0,μ1).\displaystyle\langle\psi^{0}-\psi^{1}|\mu^{1}-\mu^{0}\rangle\leq\diam(\mathcal{X})\mathrm{W}_{1}(\mu^{0},\mu^{1}).

Now notice that if μ1\mu^{1} is absolutely continuous with respect to μ0\mu^{0}, then we have for any constant c∈ℝc\in\mathbb{R}:

⟨ψ0−ψ1|μ1−μ0⟩\displaystyle\langle\psi^{0}-\psi^{1}|\mu^{1}-\mu^{0}\rangle =⟨ψ0−ψ1−c|μ1−μ0⟩\displaystyle=\langle\psi^{0}-\psi^{1}-c|\mu^{1}-\mu^{0}\rangle
=∫ℝd(ψ0−ψ1−c)​(d​μ1d​μ0−1)​d​μ0\displaystyle=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}(\psi^{0}-\psi^{1}-c)(\frac{\mathrm{d}\mu^{1}}{\mathrm{d}\mu^{0}}-1)\mathrm{d}\mu^{0}
≤(∫ℝd(ψ0−ψ1−c)2​d​μ0)1/2​(∫ℝd(d​μ1d​μ0−1)2​d​μ0)1/2\displaystyle\leq\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}(\psi^{0}-\psi^{1}-c)^{2}\mathrm{d}\mu^{0}\right)^{1/2}\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}(\frac{\mathrm{d}\mu^{1}}{\mathrm{d}\mu^{0}}-1)^{2}\mathrm{d}\mu^{0}\right)^{1/2}
=‖ψ0−ψ1−c‖L2​(μ0)​Dχ2​(μ1|μ0)1/2\displaystyle=\left\lVert\psi^{0}-\psi^{1}-c\right\rVert_{\mathrm{L}^{2}(\mu^{0})}D_{\chi^{2}}(\mu^{1}|\mu^{0})^{1/2}
≤2​‖ψ0−ψ1−c‖L2​(12​(μ0+μ1))​Dχ2​(μ1|μ0)1/2.\displaystyle\leq\sqrt{2}\left\lVert\psi^{0}-\psi^{1}-c\right\rVert_{\mathrm{L}^{2}(\frac{1}{2}(\mu^{0}+\mu^{1}))}D_{\chi^{2}}(\mu^{1}|\mu^{0})^{1/2}.

The second estimate comes after minimizing with respect to cc in the last inequality:

⟨ψ0−ψ1|μ1−μ0⟩\displaystyle\langle\psi^{0}-\psi^{1}|\mu^{1}-\mu^{0}\rangle ≤2​Var12​(μ0+μ1)​(ψ1−ψ0)1/2​Dχ2​(μ1|μ0)1/2.∎\displaystyle\leq\sqrt{2}\Var_{\frac{1}{2}(\mu^{0}+\mu^{1})}(\psi^{1}-\psi^{0})^{1/2}D_{\chi^{2}}(\mu^{1}|\mu^{0})^{1/2}.\qed
Proof of Proposition 3.1.

Let A={x∈𝒳∣ϕ1​(x)≥ϕ0​(x)}A=\{x\in\mathcal{X}\mid\phi^{1}(x)\geq\phi^{0}(x)\} and let x∈Ax\in A where ϕ1\phi^{1} is differentiable. The Fenchel-Young inequality (and equality) give:

ψ0​(∇ϕ1​(x))≥⟨x|∇ϕ1​(x)⟩−ϕ0​(x)=ψ1​(∇ϕ1​(x))+ϕ1​(x)−ϕ0​(x),\psi^{0}(\nabla\phi^{1}(x))\geq\langle x|\nabla\phi^{1}(x)\rangle-\phi^{0}(x)=\psi^{1}(\nabla\phi^{1}(x))+\phi^{1}(x)-\phi^{0}(x),

which thus ensures that for almost every x∈Ax\in A,

ψ0​(∇ϕ1​(x))−ψ1​(∇ϕ1​(x))≥ϕ1​(x)−ϕ0​(x)≥0.\psi^{0}(\nabla\phi^{1}(x))-\psi^{1}(\nabla\phi^{1}(x))\geq\phi^{1}(x)-\phi^{0}(x)\geq 0.

Similarly, for almost every x∈𝒳∖Ax\in\mathcal{X}\setminus A, we have

ψ1​(∇ϕ0​(x))−ψ0​(∇ϕ0​(x))≥ϕ0​(x)−ϕ1​(x)≥0.\psi^{1}(\nabla\phi^{0}(x))-\psi^{0}(\nabla\phi^{0}(x))\geq\phi^{0}(x)-\phi^{1}(x)\geq 0.

From this, we deduce the first statement of the proposition:

∥ψ1−ψ0\displaystyle\|\psi^{1}-\psi^{0} ∥Lp​(μ0+μ1)p=∫𝒳(|(ψ1−ψ0)∘(∇ϕ0)|p+|(ψ1−ψ0)∘(∇ϕ1)|p)dρ\displaystyle\|_{\mathrm{L}^{p}(\mu^{0}+\mu^{1})}^{p}=\int_{\mathcal{X}}\left(\left|(\psi^{1}-\psi^{0})\circ(\nabla\phi^{0})\right|^{p}+\left|(\psi^{1}-\psi^{0})\circ(\nabla\phi^{1})\right|^{p}\right)\mathrm{d}\rho
≥∫𝒳∖A(ψ1​(∇ϕ0)−ψ0​(∇ϕ0))p​𝑑ρ+∫A(ψ0​(∇ϕ1)−ψ1​(∇ϕ1))p​𝑑ρ\displaystyle\geq\int_{\mathcal{X}\setminus A}\big(\psi^{1}(\nabla\phi^{0})-\psi^{0}(\nabla\phi^{0})\big)^{p}\mathrm{d}\rho+\int_{A}\big(\psi^{0}(\nabla\phi^{1})-\psi^{1}(\nabla\phi^{1})\big)^{p}\mathrm{d}\rho
≥∫𝒳∖A(ϕ0−ϕ1)p​𝑑ρ+∫A(ϕ1−ϕ0)p​𝑑ρ=‖ϕ1−ϕ0‖Lp​(ρ)p.\displaystyle\geq\int_{\mathcal{X}\setminus A}\big(\phi^{0}-\phi^{1}\big)^{p}\mathrm{d}\rho+\int_{A}\big(\phi^{1}-\phi^{0}\big)^{p}\mathrm{d}\rho=\left\lVert\phi^{1}-\phi^{0}\right\rVert^{p}_{\mathrm{L}^{p}(\rho)}.

Let c∈ℝc\in\mathbb{R}. Having established the previous inequality for any convex functions ϕ0,ϕ1\phi^{0},\phi^{1} on 𝒳\mathcal{X}, we may replace ϕ0\phi^{0} with ϕ0−c\phi^{0}-c in this inequality, and consequently replace ψ0\psi^{0} with (ϕ0−c)∗=ψ0+c(\phi^{0}-c)^{*}=\psi^{0}+c. This yields thus for any c∈ℝc\in\mathbb{R},

‖ϕ1−ϕ0+c‖Lp​(ρ)≤‖ψ1−ψ0−c‖Lp​(μ0+μ1).\left\lVert\phi^{1}-\phi^{0}+c\right\rVert_{\mathrm{L}^{p}(\rho)}\leq\left\lVert\psi^{1}-\psi^{0}-c\right\rVert_{\mathrm{L}^{p}(\mu^{0}+\mu^{1})}.

Taking cc that achieves the minimum on the right-hand side, for p=2p=2, we get

12​Varρ⁡(ϕ1−ϕ0)\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\Var_{\rho}(\phi^{1}-\phi^{0}) ≤12​‖ϕ1−ϕ0+c‖L2​(ρ)2\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert\phi^{1}-\phi^{0}+c\right\rVert^{2}_{\mathrm{L}^{2}(\rho)}
≤‖ψ1−ψ0−c‖L2​(12​(μ0+μ1))2=Var12​(μ0+μ1)⁡(ψ1−ψ0).∎\displaystyle\leq\left\lVert\psi^{1}-\psi^{0}-c\right\rVert^{2}_{\mathrm{L}^{2}(\frac{1}{2}(\mu^{0}+\mu^{1}))}=\Var_{\frac{1}{2}(\mu^{0}+\mu^{1})}(\psi^{1}-\psi^{0}).\qed

All the stability estimates that have been established so far involve the oscillation of the Brenier potentials Mϕ−mϕM_{\phi}-m_{\phi}. It is then natural to wonder under what assumption on a measure μ∈𝒫2​(ℝd)\mu\in\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) can we control this oscillation. The next proposition, found in [7], shows that a sufficient condition is that μ\mu admits a finite moment of order p>dp>d. This assumption seems nearly tight : Remark 3.2 below shows that there exists a measure μ\mu such that Mp​(μ)<+∞M_{p}(\mu)<+\infty with p<dp<d, whose associated Brenier potential is unbounded.

Proposition 3.3 (Proposition 2.22 in [7]).

Let ρ\rho be a probability density over a compact convex set 𝒳\mathcal{X}, satisfying 0<mρ≤ρ≤Mρ0<m_{\rho}\leq\rho\leq M_{\rho} and let μ∈𝒫2​(ℝd)\mu\in\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}). Denote ϕ\phi the Brenier potential for the quadratic optimal transport between ρ\rho and μ\mu. Assume that there exists p>dp>d and Mp<+∞M_{p}<+\infty such that

Mp​(μ)=∫ℝd‖y‖p​𝑑μ​(y)≤Mp.M_{p}(\mu)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\left\lVert y\right\rVert^{p}\mathrm{d}\mu(y)\leq M_{p}.

Then ϕ\phi is Hölder continuous and verifies for all x,x′∈𝒳x,x^{\prime}\in\mathcal{X}:

|ϕ⁡(x)−ϕ⁡(x′)|≤Cd,p,𝒳​(Mpmρ)1/p​‖x−x′‖1−dp.\displaystyle\left|\phi(x)-\phi(x^{\prime})\right|\leq C_{d,p,\mathcal{X}}\left(\frac{M_{p}}{m_{\rho}}\right)^{1/p}\left\lVert x-x^{\prime}\right\rVert^{1-\frac{d}{p}}.

In particular, there exists mϕ,Mϕ∈ℝm_{\phi},M_{\phi}\in\mathbb{R} that can be chosen such that for any x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X}, mϕ≤ϕ⁡(x)≤Mϕm_{\phi}\leq\phi(x)\leq M_{\phi} and such that

Mϕ−mϕ≤Cd,p,𝒳​(Mpmρ)1/p​diam⁡(𝒳)1−dp.M_{\phi}-m_{\phi}\leq C_{d,p,\mathcal{X}}\left(\frac{M_{p}}{m_{\rho}}\right)^{1/p}\diam(\mathcal{X})^{1-\frac{d}{p}}.

Corollary 3.2 and Proposition 3.3 together imply the following.

Corollary 3.4 (Stability with enough moments).

Let ρ\rho be a probability density over a compact convex set 𝒳\mathcal{X}, satisfying 0<mρ≤ρ≤Mρ0<m_{\rho}\leq\rho\leq M_{\rho}. For any μ∈𝒫2​(ℝd)\mu\in\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}), denote ϕμ\phi_{\mu} the Brenier potential for the optimal transport between ρ\rho and μ\mu. Let p>dp>d. Then the restriction of the mapping μ↦ϕμ\mu\mapsto\phi_{\mu} to the set of probability measures with bounded pp-th moment is 1/21/2-Hölder with respect to the W1\mathrm{W}_{1} distance. More precisely, if max⁡(Mp​(μ0),Mp​(μ1))≤Mp<+∞,\max(M_{p}(\mu^{0}),M_{p}(\mu^{1}))\leq M_{p}<+\infty, then

‖ϕμ1−ϕμ0‖L2​(ρ)≤Cd,p,𝒳,ρ,Mp​W1​(μ0,μ1)1/2.\left\lVert\phi_{\mu^{1}}-\phi_{\mu^{0}}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{L}^{2}(\rho)}\leq C_{d,p,\mathcal{X},\rho,M_{p}}\mathrm{W}_{1}(\mu^{0},\mu^{1})^{1/2}.
Remark 3.1.

A large class of probability distributions admit a finite moment of order p>dp>d. For instance, sub-exponential measures, which encompass most of the commonly used heavy-tailed distributions fall into this class. We say that a measure μ∈𝒫⁡(ℝd)\mu\in\mathcal{P}\left(\mathbb{R}^{d}\right) is sub-exponential with variance proxy σ2\sigma^{2} for σ>0\sigma>0 if it has zero mean and if for all r>0r>0,

μ({x∈ℝd∣‖x‖≥r})≤2e−2r/σ.\mu(\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\mid\left\lVert x\right\rVert\geq r\})\leq 2e^{-2r/\sigma}.

We refer to Proposition 2.7.1 in [35] for equivalent characterization. The moments of such a measure are all bounded, and more precisely,

Mp​(μ)≤2​p!​(σ2)p.M_{p}(\mu)\leq 2p!\left(\frac{\sigma}{2}\right)^{p}.

We report the proof of Proposition 3.3 from [7] for completeness.

Proof of Proposition 3.3.

The gradient ∇ϕ\nabla\phi corresponds to the optimal transport map between ρ\rho and μ\mu. Using that μ\mu is the image of ρ\rho under ∇ϕ\nabla\phi, the moment assumption gives,

‖∇ϕ‖Lp​(𝒳)p\displaystyle\left\lVert\nabla\phi\right\rVert_{\mathrm{L}^{p}(\mathcal{X})}^{p} =∫𝒳‖∇ϕ​(x)‖p​𝑑x≤1mρ​∫𝒳‖∇ϕ​(x)‖p​𝑑ρ​(x)≤Mpmρ.\displaystyle=\int_{\mathcal{X}}\left\lVert\nabla\phi(x)\right\rVert^{p}\mathrm{d}x\leq\frac{1}{m_{\rho}}\int_{\mathcal{X}}\left\lVert\nabla\phi(x)\right\rVert^{p}\mathrm{d}\rho(x)\leq\frac{M_{p}}{m_{\rho}}.

We can add a constant to ϕ\phi so that ∫𝒳ϕ⁡(x)​𝑑x=0\int_{\mathcal{X}}\phi(x)\mathrm{d}x=0 without changing its modulus of continuity. The Poincaré-Wirtinger inequality then ensures that ‖ϕ‖Lp​(𝒳)≤Cp,𝒳​‖∇ϕ‖Lp​(𝒳).\left\lVert\phi\right\rVert_{\mathrm{L}^{p}(\mathcal{X})}\leq C_{p,\mathcal{X}}\left\lVert\nabla\phi\right\rVert_{\mathrm{L}^{p}(\mathcal{X})}. In particular, the potential ϕ\phi belongs to the Sobolev space W1,p​(𝒳)W^{1,p}(\mathcal{X}). Morrey’s inequality (Theorem 11.34 and Theorem 12.15 in [25]) ensures that ϕ\phi is (1−dp)(1-\frac{d}{p})-Hölder and that there exists a constant depending only on d,pd,p and 𝒳\mathcal{X} such that

∀x≠x′∈𝒳,|ϕ⁡(x)−ϕ⁡(x′)|‖x−x′‖1−dp\displaystyle\forall x\neq x^{\prime}\in\mathcal{X},\quad\frac{\left|\phi(x)-\phi(x^{\prime})\right|}{\left\lVert x-x^{\prime}\right\rVert^{1-\frac{d}{p}}} ≤Cd,p,𝒳​‖ϕ‖W1,p​(𝒳)≤Cd,p,𝒳​(Mpmρ)1/p.∎\displaystyle\leq C_{d,p,\mathcal{X}}\left\lVert\phi\right\rVert_{W^{1,p}(\mathcal{X})}\leq C_{d,p,\mathcal{X}}\left(\frac{M_{p}}{m_{\rho}}\right)^{1/p}.\qed
Remark 3.2 (Morrey’s inequality for convex functions).

Since the Brenier potentials ϕ\phi are convex, one may wonder whether Morrey’s inequality and the resulting Sobolev embedding can be improved when restrictected to the class of convex functions. However, one can show that for 𝒳=[0,1]d\mathcal{X}=[0,1]^{d} and p<dp<d, for α∈(0,dp−1)\alpha\in\left(0,\frac{d}{p}-1\right), the potential

ϕ:{𝒳→ℝ(x1,…,xd)↦(x1+⋯+xd)−α\phi:\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}\\ (x_{1},\dots,x_{d})\mapsto(x_{1}+\dots+x_{d})^{-\alpha}\end{array}\right.

is convex, belongs to W1,p​(𝒳)W^{1,p}(\mathcal{X}), but obviously neither Hölder continuous nor even bounded. In other words, assuming that Mp​(μ)<+∞M_{p}(\mu)<+\infty for p<dp<d does not guarantee that the Brenier potential from ρ\rho to μ\mu is α\alpha-Hölder, or even bounded.

4. Stability of optimal transport maps

In this section, we derive quantitative stability estimates on optimal transport maps with respect to the target measures from the stability estimates on Brenier potentials given in the preceding section. This derivation relies on a Gagliardo–Nirenberg type inequality on the difference of convex functions, which is reported here but will be proven in Section 5.

Proposition 4.1.

Let KK be a compact domain of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} with rectifiable boundary and let u,v:K→ℝu,v:K\to\mathbb{R} be two LL-Lipschitz functions on KK that are convex on any segment included in KK. Then there exists a constant CdC_{d} depending only on dd such that

‖∇u−∇v‖L2​(K,ℝd)2≤Cd​ℋd−1​(∂K)2/3​L4/3​‖u−v‖L2​(K)2/3,\left\lVert\nabla u-\nabla v\right\rVert_{\mathrm{L}^{2}(K,\mathbb{R}^{d})}^{2}\leq C_{d}\mathcal{H}^{d-1}(\partial K)^{2/3}L^{4/3}\left\lVert u-v\right\rVert^{2/3}_{\mathrm{L}^{2}(K)},

where ℋd−1\mathcal{H}^{d-1} denotes the (d−1)(d-1)-dimensional Hausdorff measure.

With this proposition at hand, the stability result for Brenier potentials can readily be transferred to stability of the corresponding optimal transport maps – that is, to their gradient – at least when the target measures are compactly supported. Indeed, Proposition 4.1 together with Corollary 3.2 directly imply:

Theorem 4.2 (Stability of the Brenier map, compact case).

Let 𝒳,𝒴\mathcal{X},\mathcal{Y} be compact subsets of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} with 𝒳\mathcal{X} convex, let ρ\rho be a probability density over 𝒳\mathcal{X} bounded from above and below by positive constants and let μ0,μ1∈𝒫⁡(𝒴)\mu^{0},\mu^{1}\in\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Y}). Denoting TμkT_{\mu^{k}} the Brenier map from ρ\rho to μk\mu^{k}, we have

W2​(μ0,μ1)≤‖Tμ0−Tμ1‖L2​(ρ,ℝd)≤Cd,ρ,𝒳,𝒴​W1​(μ0,μ1)16.\mathrm{W}_{2}(\mu^{0},\mu^{1})\leq\left\lVert T_{\mu^{0}}-T_{\mu^{1}}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{L}^{2}(\rho,\mathbb{R}^{d})}\leq C_{d,\rho,\mathcal{X},\mathcal{Y}}\mathrm{W}_{1}(\mu^{0},\mu^{1})^{\frac{1}{6}}.

In particular, the embedding μ∈𝒫2​(𝒴)→Tμ∈L2​(ρ,ℝd)\mu\in\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathcal{Y})\to T_{\mu}\in\mathrm{L}^{2}(\rho,\mathbb{R}^{d}) is bi-Hölder continuous.

Remark 4.1 (bi-Hölder embedding via potentials).

The previous theorem and Proposition 4.1 together with Corollary 3.2 also ensure the following bi-Hölder behavior for the Brenier potentials (with zero mean against ρ\rho on 𝒳\mathcal{X}):

∀μ0,μ1∈𝒫⁡(𝒴),W2​(μ0,μ1)3≲‖ϕ1−ϕ0‖L2​(ρ)≲W1​(μ0,μ1)12,\forall\mu^{0},\mu^{1}\in\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Y}),\quad\mathrm{W}_{2}(\mu^{0},\mu^{1})^{3}\lesssim\left\lVert\phi^{1}-\phi^{0}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{L}^{2}(\rho)}\lesssim\mathrm{W}_{1}(\mu^{0},\mu^{1})^{\frac{1}{2}},

where the ≲\lesssim notation hides multiplicative constants depending on d,ρ,𝒳,𝒴d,\rho,\mathcal{X},\mathcal{Y}.

We now phrase a similar stability result for probability measures whose Brenier potential is Hölder continuous and that admit a bounded fourth order moment. This includes a large class of probability measures, as noticed in Proposition 3.3 and Remark 3.1.

Theorem 4.3 (Stability of the Brenier map).

Let ρ\rho be a probability density over a compact convex set 𝒳⊂ℝd\mathcal{X}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}, satisfying 0<mρ≤ρ≤Mρ0<m_{\rho}\leq\rho\leq M_{\rho}. Assume that there exists Mα>0M_{\alpha}>0 and α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1) such that for all x,x′∈𝒳x,x^{\prime}\in\mathcal{X} and k∈{0,1}k\in\{0,1\},

|ϕk​(x)−ϕk​(x′)|≤Mα​‖x−x′‖α.\left|\phi^{k}(x)-\phi^{k}(x^{\prime})\right|\leq M_{\alpha}\left\lVert x-x^{\prime}\right\rVert^{\alpha}.

Assume that there exists 0<M<+∞0<M<+\infty such that for k∈{0,1}k\in\{0,1\}, M4​(μk)≤M.M_{4}(\mu^{k})\leq M. Then

(15) W2​(μ0,μ1)≤‖∇ϕ1−∇ϕ0‖L2​(ρ,ℝd)≤Cd,ρ,𝒳,α,Mα,M​W1​(μ0,μ1)12​(11−8​α).\mathrm{W}_{2}(\mu^{0},\mu^{1})\leq\left\lVert\nabla\phi^{1}-\nabla\phi^{0}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{L}^{2}(\rho,\mathbb{R}^{d})}\leq C_{d,\rho,\mathcal{X},\alpha,M_{\alpha},M}\mathrm{W}_{1}(\mu^{0},\mu^{1})^{\frac{1}{2(11-8\alpha)}}.
Remark 4.2.

The assumption M4​(μk)<+∞M_{4}(\mu^{k})<+\infty comes from a use of the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality in the proof of Theorem 4.3. However, one could use Hölder’s inequality instead, under different moment assumption and show that for any q≥1q\geq 1, assuming that M2​q​(μk)≤M2​q<+∞M_{2q}(\mu^{k})\leq M_{2q}<+\infty for k∈{0,1}k\in\{0,1\}, one has

‖∇ϕ1−∇ϕ0‖L2​(ρ)≤Cd,ρ,𝒳,Mα,α,M2​q​W1​(μ0,μ1)q−12​(q​(7−4​α)−3).\left\lVert\nabla\phi^{1}-\nabla\phi^{0}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{L}^{2}(\rho)}\leq C_{d,\rho,\mathcal{X},M_{\alpha},\alpha,M_{2q}}\mathrm{W}_{1}(\mu^{0},\mu^{1})^{\frac{q-1}{2(q(7-4\alpha)-3)}}.

Since the exponent is an increasing function of qq, a stronger stability can be obtained at the cost of stronger moment assumptions.

Theorem 4.3 and Proposition 3.3 directly imply the following.

Corollary 4.4 (Stability with enough moments).

Let ρ\rho be a probability density over a compact convex set 𝒳⊂ℝd\mathcal{X}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}, satisfying 0<mρ≤ρ≤Mρ0<m_{\rho}\leq\rho\leq M_{\rho}. For μ∈𝒫2​(ℝd)\mu\in\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}), denote ∇ϕμ\nabla\phi_{\mu} the optimal transport map for the quadratic optimal transport between ρ\rho and μ\mu. Let p∈ℝp\in\mathbb{R} and assume p≥4p\geq 4 and p>dp>d. Then, the map μ↦Tμ\mu\mapsto T_{\mu} is Hölder when restricted to the set of probability measures with bounded pp-th moment. More precisely, if max⁡(Mp​(μ0),Mp​(μ1))≤Mp<+∞,\max(M_{p}(\mu^{0}),M_{p}(\mu^{1}))\leq M_{p}<+\infty, then

W2​(μ0,μ1)≤‖∇ϕμ1−∇ϕμ0‖L2​(ρ,ℝd)≤Cd,p,𝒳,ρ,Mp​W1​(μ0,μ1)p6​p+16​d.\mathrm{W}_{2}(\mu^{0},\mu^{1})\leq\left\lVert\nabla\phi_{\mu^{1}}-\nabla\phi_{\mu^{0}}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{L}^{2}(\rho,\mathbb{R}^{d})}\leq C_{d,p,\mathcal{X},\rho,M_{p}}\mathrm{W}_{1}(\mu^{0},\mu^{1})^{\frac{p}{6p+16d}}.

To prove Theorem 4.3, we first show that whenever a Brenier potential defined on the compact and convex set 𝒳\mathcal{X} is Hölder continuous, it is possible to control its Lipschitz constant on erosions of 𝒳\mathcal{X}. We recall that for η>0\eta>0, the η\eta-erosion of 𝒳\mathcal{X}, denoted 𝒳−η\mathcal{X}_{-\eta}, corresponds to the set of points of 𝒳\mathcal{X} that are at least at a distance η\eta from ∂𝒳\partial\mathcal{X}. The proof of this proposition is inspired by Proposition 3.3 in [20].

Proposition 4.5 (Lipschitz behavior on erosion).

Let ρ\rho be a probability density over a compact convex set 𝒳⊂ℝd\mathcal{X}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}, satisfying 0<mρ≤ρ≤Mρ0<m_{\rho}\leq\rho\leq M_{\rho}. Let μ∈𝒫2​(ℝd)\mu\in\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) and denote ϕ\phi the Brenier potential for the quadratic optimal transport between ρ\rho and μ\mu. Assume that there exists Mα>0M_{\alpha}>0 and α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1) such that for all x,x′∈𝒳x,x^{\prime}\in\mathcal{X},

|ϕ⁡(x)−ϕ⁡(x′)|≤Mα​‖x−x′‖α.\left|\phi(x)-\phi(x^{\prime})\right|\leq M_{\alpha}\left\lVert x-x^{\prime}\right\rVert^{\alpha}.

Then, ϕ\phi is RR-Lipschitz on the erosion 𝒳−ηR\mathcal{X}_{-\eta_{R}} with ηR=(MαR)11−α\eta_{R}=\left(\frac{M_{\alpha}}{R}\right)^{\frac{1}{1-\alpha}}.

Let x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X} be such that d⁡(x,∂𝒳)≥ηRd(x,\partial\mathcal{X})\geq\eta_{R}, and let g∈∂ϕ⁡(x)g\in\partial\phi(x). We will show that ‖g‖≤R\left\lVert g\right\rVert\leq R, thus implying the statement. Denoting ψ=(ϕ)∗\psi=(\phi)^{*}, the Fenchel-Young equality and inequality ensures that

{ψ⁡(g)=⟨g|x⟩−ϕ⁡(x),ψ⁡(g)≥⟨g|x′⟩−ϕ⁡(x′) for all ​x′∈𝒳.\begin{cases}\psi(g)=\langle g|x\rangle-\phi(x),\\ \psi(g)\geq\langle g|x^{\prime}\rangle-\phi(x^{\prime})&\hbox{ for all }x^{\prime}\in\mathcal{X}.\end{cases}

Putting these equations together, we get that for any x′∈𝒳x^{\prime}\in\mathcal{X},

(16) ⟨g|x′−x⟩≤ϕ⁡(x′)−ϕ⁡(x)≤Mα​‖x′−x‖α,\displaystyle\langle g|x^{\prime}-x\rangle\leq\phi(x^{\prime})-\phi(x)\leq M_{\alpha}\left\lVert x^{\prime}-x\right\rVert^{\alpha},

Proposition 4.5 allows to control the Lipschitz constant of the restriction ϕk\phi^{k} to 𝒳−η\mathcal{X}_{-\eta} assuming that ϕk\phi^{k} is α\alpha-Hölder continuous. Combining it with the inequality of Proposition 4.1, we get a stability estimate for the restriction of the transport map to 𝒳−η\mathcal{X}_{-\eta}. To conclude the proof of the theorem, we will rely on an upper bound on the volume of the symetric difference betwen 𝒳\mathcal{X} and its erosion 𝒳−η\mathcal{X}_{-\eta} given in the next proposition.

Let 𝒳⊂ℝd\mathcal{X}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} be a compact convex set containing the origin, and denote r𝒳>0r_{\mathcal{X}}>0 and R𝒳>0R_{\mathcal{X}}>0 the largest and smallest radii such that B⁡(0,r𝒳)⊆𝒳⊆B⁡(0,R𝒳)B(0,r_{\mathcal{X}})\subseteq\mathcal{X}\subseteq B(0,R_{\mathcal{X}}). Lemma 4.7 (Lemma 1 in [26]).

For all η≤r𝒳\eta\leq r_{\mathcal{X}}, vold​(𝒳\𝒳−η)≤vold​(𝒳+η\𝒳).\mathrm{vol}^{d}(\mathcal{X}\backslash\mathcal{X}_{-\eta})\leq\mathrm{vol}^{d}(\mathcal{X}_{+\eta}\backslash\mathcal{X}).

Corollary 4.8.

Let 𝒳,𝒴\mathcal{X},\mathcal{Y} be compact subsets of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, and assume that 𝒳\mathcal{X} is convex and that 𝒴\mathcal{Y} has a rectifiable boundary. Let ρ\rho be a probability density over 𝒳\mathcal{X} satisfying 0<mρ≤ρ≤Mρ<+∞0<m_{\rho}\leq\rho\leq M_{\rho}<+\infty and let μ0,μ1\mu^{0},\mu^{1} be probability densities over 𝒴\mathcal{Y} satisfying

∀k∈{0,1},0<cμ≤μk≤Cμ<+∞.\forall k\in\{0,1\},\quad 0<c_{\mu}\leq\mu^{k}\leq C_{\mu}<+\infty.

Assume that μ0\mu^{0} and μ1\mu^{1} are absolutely continuous measures on the compact 𝒴\mathcal{Y}, whose densities are bounded by a common constant CμC_{\mu}. Then, for any function f∈H1​(𝒴)f\in H^{1}(\mathcal{Y}), we have the following inequality:

5. Gagliardo–Nirenberg type inequality for difference of convex functions

We prove here Proposition 4.1, a sort of reverse Poincaré inequality which allows to control the L2\mathrm{L}^{2} distance ‖∇u−∇v‖L2​(K,ℝd)\left\lVert\nabla u-\nabla v\right\rVert_{\mathrm{L}^{2}(K,\mathbb{R}^{d})} between the gradients of Lipschitz convex functions u,vu,v using the L2\mathrm{L}^{2} distance beween these functions ‖u−v‖L2​(K)\left\lVert u-v\right\rVert_{\mathrm{L}^{2}(K)}. This proposition is a refinement of Theorem 3.5 in [14], in which the upper bound involved the uniform distance ‖u−v‖∞\left\lVert u-v\right\rVert_{\infty}. Proposition 4.1 is first proven in dimension d=1d=1 and on a segment (Lemma 5.1) and then generalized to higher dimensions using arguments from integral geometry.

Remark 5.1 (Relation to the Gagliardo–Nirenberg inequality).

Although the estimate of Proposition 4.1 resembles the Gagliardo–Nirenberg inequality, it cannot be deduced form it. More precisely, we note that without convexity of uu and vv, the inequality in (4.1) does not hold. One can see this by taking u=0u=0 and vn​(x)=1n​sin⁡(n​x)v_{n}(x)=\frac{1}{n}\sin(nx) on K=[0,1]K=[0,1].

Remark 5.2 (Optimality of exponents).

The inequality proposed in Proposition 4.1 is sharp in term of the exponents of LL and ‖u−v‖L2​(K)\left\lVert u-v\right\rVert_{\mathrm{L}^{2}(K)} in the right-hand side. In the case d=1d=1, let L>0,ε>0L>0,\varepsilon>0 and define on K=[0,1]K=[0,1], u⁡(x)=L​|x−12|u(x)=L|x-\frac{1}{2}| and v=max⁡(u,ε)v=\max(u,\varepsilon). Then u,vu,v are convex and LL-Lipschitz and we have:

‖u−v‖L2​([0,1])2=23​ε3Land‖u′−v′‖L2​([0,1])2=2​L​ε.\displaystyle\left\lVert u-v\right\rVert^{2}_{\mathrm{L}^{2}([0,1])}=\frac{2}{3}\frac{\varepsilon^{3}}{L}\quad\text{and}\quad\left\lVert u^{\prime}-v^{\prime}\right\rVert^{2}_{\mathrm{L}^{2}([0,1])}=2L\varepsilon.

so that ‖u′−v′‖L2​([0,1])2=121/3​L4/3​‖u−v‖L2​([0,1])2/3.\left\lVert u^{\prime}-v^{\prime}\right\rVert^{2}_{\mathrm{L}^{2}([0,1])}=12^{1/3}L^{4/3}\left\lVert u-v\right\rVert^{2/3}_{\mathrm{L}^{2}([0,1])}.

Let I⊂ℝI\subset\mathbb{R} be a compact segment and let u,v:I→ℝu,v:I\to\mathbb{R} be two convex functions with uniformly bounded gradients on II. Then

(22) ‖u′−v′‖L2​(I)2≤8​(‖u′‖L∞​(I)+‖v′‖L∞​(I))4/3​‖u−v‖L2​(I)2/3.\left\lVert u^{\prime}-v^{\prime}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{L}^{2}(I)}^{2}\leq 8(\left\lVert u^{\prime}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{L}^{\infty}(I)}+\left\lVert v^{\prime}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{L}^{\infty}(I)})^{4/3}\left\lVert u-v\right\rVert_{\mathrm{L}^{2}(I)}^{2/3}.

The one-dimensional result from Lemma 5.1 is generalized to higher dimensions thanks to two formulas from integral geometry that allow to rewrite the L2\mathrm{L}^{2} norms of the scalar-field u−vu-v and vector-field ∇u−∇v\nabla u-\nabla v over set K⊂ℝdK\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} using integrals over lines intersecting KK.

Integral geometry

Denote 𝒮d−1\mathcal{S}^{d-1} the unit sphere in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, and let σ\sigma be the uniform probability measure on it. We denote {e}⟂\{e\}^{\perp} the hyperplane orthogonal to a unit vector ee. ≤(∫e∈𝒮d−1∫{e}⟂nℓey​d​ℋd−1​(y)​𝑑σ​(e))2/3​‖u−v‖L2​(K)2/3.\displaystyle\leq\left(\int_{e\in\mathcal{S}^{d-1}}\int_{\{e\}^{\perp}}n_{\ell^{y}_{e}}\mathrm{d}\mathcal{H}^{d-1}(y)\mathrm{d}\sigma(e)\right)^{2/3}\left\lVert u-v\right\rVert_{\mathrm{L}^{2}(K)}^{2/3}.

The conclusion comes after using again that nℓey≤#⁡(ℓey∩∂K)n_{\ell^{y}_{e}}\leq\#(\ell^{y}_{e}\cap\partial K) and Crofton’s formula (26)

∫e∈𝒮d−1∫{e}⟂nℓey​d​ℋd−1​(y)​𝑑σ​(e)≤1Cd′​ℋd−1​(∂K).∎\int_{e\in\mathcal{S}^{d-1}}\int_{\{e\}^{\perp}}n_{\ell^{y}_{e}}\mathrm{d}\mathcal{H}^{d-1}(y)\mathrm{d}\sigma(e)\leq\frac{1}{C_{d}^{\prime}}\mathcal{H}^{d-1}(\partial K).\qed
